opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it was just honesty. He's someone who's always been very transparent with his students, and he knew that if he made a move like that, it would affect the people who were working closely with him, me included. So rather than having it come as a surprise, he wanted me to understand where his head was at and why.

And I think there was also a mentoring element. At that point the line between academic math and AI research was starting to blur. A lot of people who'd spent their careers proving theorems were looking at what the large models could do and asking, "Is this where the frontier is moving?" I think he wanted me to see that this wasn't him abandoning mathematics. In his view it was a way of following where the interesting problems were going. Talking it through with me was a way of saying: you should think about this too, about where you want to be in five or ten years.

Honestly, those conversations shaped a lot of my own thinking. They made me take seriously the idea that you could work on formal reasoning and AI not as a side project, but as the main thing. So in a way, preparing me for his possible move was also preparing me for my own.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the teacher’s transparency and mentorship about the shift toward AI research, but does not say OpenAI’s AI-for-math work could compete strategically with Hong’s company, Axiom.

fable-5.1.text:
I think he saw it coming earlier than I did. When he first raised it with me, it wasn't framed as "I'm leaving," it was more like, "you need to understand that the center of gravity is shifting." He was watching what was happening at the frontier labs, and he knew that the kind of research he cared about was increasingly going to be done with resources that no university group could match. So I think part of it was honesty. He didn't want me to wake up one day and discover that my advisor was gone and that I hadn't been told.

But I also think it was a kind of training. He wanted me to be able to stand on my own intellectually, without him in the room. A lot of advisors, consciously or not, make their students dependent on them. He did the opposite. He pushed me to pick problems I could defend by myself, to build relationships with other people in the field, to know what I believed independently of what he believed. In hindsight, the conversations about OpenAI were really conversations about "what do you do when the person you've been leaning on is no longer there?"

And honestly, it changed how I thought about my own path. If the most serious work was going to happen inside these organizations, then I had to ask myself whether I wanted to join one, or whether I wanted to build something myself. I don't think I would have arrived at Axiom as quickly if he hadn't forced me to sit with that question so early.
